entry: Color at the long-wavelength end of the visible spectrum, next to orange. Its dominant wavelength is approximately 625–750 nanometers. It is a [[Primary color|primary color]] in the [[RGB color model]] and a secondary color, made from magenta and yellow, in the [[CMYK color model]]. It is the complementary color of [[Cyan|cyan]]. Reds range from yellow-tinged scarlet and [[Vermilion|vermilion]] to bluish-red crimson, and from pale pink to dark burgundy. Red pigment made from [[Ochre|ochre]] was among the first colors used in [[Prehistoric art|prehistoric art]]. Red became a symbolic color of communism and socialism, and Soviet Russia adopted a red flag following the Bolshevik Revolution in 1917. Because red is the color of blood, it has long been associated with sacrifice, danger and courage. In China, India and many other Asian countries it symbolizes happiness and good fortune.

Largest of the true foxes and the most widely distributed member of the order [[Carnivora]]. It ranges across the Northern Hemisphere and parts of North Africa, and was introduced to Australia, where it preys on native rodents and marsupials. It originated in [[Eurasia]] during the Middle [[Pleistocene]], 400,000 years ago, and forty-six subspecies are recognized. Its predators include the [[Golden eagle|golden eagle]], and it has been extensively hunted for its [[Fur trade|fur]]. Listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, it is also on the list of the world's 100 worst invasive species. It has successfully colonized many [[Suburb|suburban]] and [[Urban area|urban]] areas.

Luminous giant star of low or intermediate mass, roughly 0.3–8 solar masses, in a late phase of stellar evolution. Its outer atmosphere is inflated and tenuous, so its radius is large and its surface temperature is around 5,000 K (4,700 °C; 8,500 °F) or lower, giving it a color from yellow-white to reddish-orange. Having exhausted the hydrogen in its core, it fuses hydrogen in a shell around an inert helium core. Red giants evolve from [[Main sequence|main-sequence]] stars. Their radii are tens to hundreds of times larger than that of the [[Sun]], and their luminosities can reach nearly three thousand times that of the Sun. Many well-known bright stars are red giants; [[Arcturus]], a K0 star on the red-giant branch, is 36 [[Light-year|light-years]] away. A red giant usually produces a [[Planetary nebula|planetary nebula]] and becomes a [[White dwarf|white dwarf]] at the end of its life.

Species of tropical galliform bird and primary ancestor of the domestic [[Chicken|chicken]]. Found across much of [[Southeast Asia]] and parts of [[South Asia]], it was formally described in 1758 by [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]]. Chickens were first [[Domestication|domesticated]] from it about 8,000 years ago. Males weigh around 1.5 kilograms (3.3 lb) and females around 1 kilogram (2.2 lb). Males have much brighter plumage than the drab females, with golden hackle feathers and a tail of iridescent feathers up to 28 centimeters (11 in) long, which suits the females' [[Camouflage|camouflage]]. The wild form is sometimes kept in zoos and parks for pest control.

Part of an urban area with a concentration of prostitution and sex-oriented businesses, such as sex shops, strip clubs and adult theaters. Such districts are particularly associated with female street [[Prostitution|prostitution]], though some coincide with male prostitution and gay venues. According to the [[Oxford English Dictionary]], the term appeared in print in 1894. Some districts, such as those in [[Amsterdam]] and [[Hamburg]], are officially designated for legal, regulated prostitution, and authorities often confined them to a single area. Japanese police once drew red lines on maps to mark the boundaries of legal districts, called *akasen*, or red-line.

Small arboreal mammal native to the eastern [[Himalayas]] and southwestern China, also called the lesser panda. It has dense reddish-brown fur, a black belly and legs, and a ringed tail, and weighs between 3.2 and 15 kg (7.1 and 33.1 lb). It is not closely related to the [[Giant panda|giant panda]], a bear; genetic evidence places it near raccoons, weasels and skunks. It feeds mainly on [[Bamboo|bamboo]] shoots and leaves, and inhabits [[Conifer|coniferous]] and [[Temperate broadleaf and mixed forests|temperate broadleaf and mixed forests]]. Listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List since 2015, it is threatened by poaching and [[Deforestation|deforestation]].

Species of tree squirrel in the [[Genus|genus]] *Sciurus*, common throughout [[Eurasia]]. An arboreal, primarily herbivorous [[Rodent|rodent]], it eats mainly [[Conifer|conifer]] seeds, nuts and fungi, and caches food in autumn. At present 23 subspecies are recognized, though the status of some is uncertain. Subspecies range from the [[Iberian Peninsula]] to the [[Lena River]] in Siberia. In 2017 a subspecies from southern [[Italy]] was elevated to species status as the Calabrian black squirrel. In the United Kingdom, introduced gray squirrels outcompete the native species and transmit squirrelpox virus, reducing British numbers to approximately 287,000, concentrated in [[Scotland]] and isolated areas.

Passerine bird of the family Icteridae found in most of North America and much of Central America. It breeds from [[Alaska]] and Newfoundland south to Florida, the [[Gulf of Mexico]], Mexico and Guatemala. Northern populations are generally migratory, while some may winter as far north as [[Pennsylvania]] and [[British Columbia]]. Claims have been made that it is the most abundant living land bird in North America: wintering flocks can exceed a million birds, and breeding pairs across North and Central America may exceed 250 million in peak years. The male is all black with a red shoulder and yellow wing bar, while the female is a nondescript dark brown. [[Seed|Seeds]] and insects make up the bulk of its diet. The species was first described as *Oriolus phoeniceus* by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1766, and its genus name *Agelaius* derives from an Ancient Greek word meaning gregarious.

Canid native to the southeastern United States, intermediate in size between the [[Coyote|coyote]] and gray wolf. Its species status has been contested for nearly a century; it has been considered either a subspecies of the gray wolf or a coywolf, a genetic admixture of coyote and wolf. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service listed it as [[Endangered species|endangered]] in 1973. As of August 2026, the wild population was estimated at approximately 22–23 adults and subadults, plus 14–15 pups, and around 295 were held in captive conservation programs.

Highly venomous spider of the widow genus [[Latrodectus]], also called the Australian black widow. Females, about 10 millimeters (0.4 in) long, are black with a red stripe on the upper abdomen and an hourglass-shaped red or orange mark underneath; males are only 3–4 mm (0.12–0.16 in) long. It preys on insects, spiders and small vertebrates from untidy webs, often inside homes. Its [[Venom|venom]] is predominantly neurotoxic to vertebrates and causes latrodectism, with pain that can persist for over 24 hours. An antivenom has been available since 1956. Colonies exist in [[New Zealand]], [[Japan]] and the United Arab Emirates.

American social news website and discussion forum. Users submit links, text, images and videos, which are voted up or down in user-created boards called subreddits. Founded in June 2005 by Steve Huffman and Alexis Ohanian, it was acquired by Condé Nast Publications in October 2006. Based in [[San Francisco]], it was ranked the ninth-most-visited website in the world as of October 2026, according to Similarweb. About 10% of its revenue comes from licensing data to [[Google]] and OpenAI for [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]] training. It has been criticized for spreading misinformation and for a voting system that can encourage echo chambers.

Chemical reaction in which the oxidation states of the reactants change. Oxidation is the loss of [[Electron|electrons]] or an increase in oxidation state; reduction is the gain of electrons or a decrease in oxidation state. The two always occur together, and the term, a portmanteau of *reduction* and *oxidation*, first appeared in a 1928 article by Leonor Michaelis and Louis B. Flexner. Redox reactions drive [[Cellular respiration|cellular respiration]] and [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]], combustion, corrosion and the reactions that power batteries. Industry uses them to extract metals from their [[Ore|ores]] by [[Smelting|smelting]], to electroplate objects and to manufacture [[Nitric acid]]. In the [[Rust|rusting]] of iron, the iron is oxidized as it converts to an [[Oxide|oxide]] and oxygen is reduced.

Increase in the wavelength, or decrease in the frequency, of electromagnetic radiation such as light. The opposite change is a blueshift. Astronomy and cosmology recognize three forms: [[Doppler effect|Doppler]] redshift from the relative motion of sources, gravitational redshift as radiation escapes a gravitational potential, and cosmological redshift caused by the [[Expansion of the universe|expansion of the universe]]. Strong redshifting can turn a gamma ray into an X-ray, and the initial 3,000 kelvin radiation of the [[Big Bang]] has redshifted to the 3 K [[Cosmic microwave background|cosmic microwave background]]. The effect is named after Christian Doppler, who offered the first known physical explanation in 1842. In 1912 Vesto Slipher found that the [[Andromeda Galaxy]] had a blueshift, indicating it was moving toward Earth. Redshift is also used in Doppler radar and radar guns.

Form of argument that establishes a claim by showing that its contrary leads to absurdity or [[Contradiction|contradiction]]. Known in Latin as *reductio ad absurdum*, it traces back to [[Ancient Greek philosophy]] and was formalized by [[Aristotle]]. In mathematics it is called proof by contradiction, and it is used in many [[Mathematical proof|proofs]], though not every school of mathematical thought accepts this nonconstructive method. [[Euclid]] used it to show the existence of [[Irrational number|irrational numbers]]. A classic example shows there is no smallest positive [[Rational number|rational number]]: if one existed, half of it would be a smaller positive rational.

Philosophical position that explains a complex system as the sum of its simpler, more fundamental parts. It is often contrasted with holism and is associated with [[Materialism|materialism]] and [[Determinism|determinism]]. The *Oxford Companion to Philosophy* calls it one of the most used and abused terms in the philosophical lexicon, and distinguishes ontological, methodological and theory reductionism. Methodological reductionism holds that the best scientific strategy is always to explain phenomena in terms of ever-smaller entities. In the sciences, the temperature of a gas is reduced to the average kinetic energy of its molecules, and some thinkers attempt to reduce biology to [[Physics|physics]] and [[Chemistry|chemistry]]. Reductionism does not preclude emergent phenomena, but implies they can be understood completely in terms of the processes from which they are composed.

American actress and producer. Witherspoon made her screen debut as a teenager in *The Man in the Moon* (1991). Her breakthrough came in 1999 with *Election*, and she gained wider recognition with *Legally Blonde* (2001). She won the Academy Award for Best Actress for playing June Carter Cash in *Walk the Line* (2005). Through her company Hello Sunshine she produced the [[HBO]] series *Big Little Lies*, which won the Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Limited Series. In 2021 [[Forbes]] named her the world's highest-paid actress. She owns Reese's Book Club and the clothing company Draper James.

Direct vote by the electorate, rather than its representatives, on a proposal, law or political issue. A referendum may be binding, adopting a new policy, or consultative, functioning like a large [[Opinion poll|opinion poll]]. The word is the Latin gerundive of *referre*, meaning to carry back, and the [[Oxford English Dictionary]] rules out the Latin plural *referenda* in favor of *referendums*. The term *plebiscite* derives from the Latin *plebiscita*, decrees of the Plebeian Council of the [[Roman Republic]]. The name and use of the referendum are thought to have originated in the Swiss canton of Graubünden in the 16th century, and [[Switzerland]] remains a prominent user. Since the 1970s its use has grown, attributed to a decline in attachment to political parties as specific policy issues became more important to the public. In [[Australia]], the terms have historically been used interchangeably.

Change in direction of a wave at an interface between two media, so that the wave returns into the medium it came from. For specular reflection, as from a [[Mirror|mirror]], the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Specular reflection forms images, while diffuse reflection from rough surfaces scatters the wave in many directions. Light also reflects from transparent surfaces such as water or glass, though less effectively. Total internal reflection occurs when light in a denser medium meets the interface at an angle greater than the critical angle; it underpins [[Fiber|fiber]]-optic communication. Reflection occurs with many kinds of wave: it causes echoes in [[Acoustics|acoustics]] and is used in [[Sonar]], it is important for [[Radio|radio]] transmission and [[Radar]], and even hard [[X-ray|X-rays]] and [[Gamma ray|gamma rays]] can be reflected at shallow angles.

Involuntary, unplanned and nearly instantaneous response to a stimulus. A stimulus initiates a neural signal that travels along a reflex arc, and these signals do not always reach the brain. The simplest reflexes involve a single synapse. The startle reflex gives an automatic response to an unexpected stimulus, and the feline righting reflex reorients a falling cat for a safe landing. Reflexes are used in [[Medicine|medicine]] to assess the [[Nervous system|nervous system]]: doctors grade them from 0 to 4, with 2+ considered normal. Decreased reflexes generally indicate a peripheral problem, and lively or exaggerated reflexes a central one. Newborn [[Infant|infants]] have primitive reflexes, such as the rooting and Moro reflexes, that are not seen in adults. Processes such as [[Breathing|breathing]] and [[Digestion|digestion]] are regarded as reflex actions under some definitions.

Major Jewish denomination, also known as Liberal or Progressive Judaism, that emphasizes the evolving nature of Jewish tradition and the primacy of its ethical aspects over ceremonial ones. It regards [[Halakha|Jewish law]] as non-binding and the individual as autonomous. Originating in mid-19th-century Germany, the early movement omitted observances and beliefs considered superstitious and translated much prayer into German. Brought to America by German-born rabbis, it flourished as Classical Reform from the 1860s to the 1930s, when most liturgy was in English and converts and male babies were not required to undergo [[Circumcision|circumcision]]. The 1937 Columbus Platform reasserted observance after the arrival of traditional Eastern European immigrants. Since the 1970s it has pursued inclusiveness and is strongly identified with progressive politics, under the motto tikkun olam. The World Union for Progressive Judaism represents at least 1.8 million people in 50 countries, making Reform the second-largest Jewish denomination after [[Orthodox Judaism]].

Economic reforms in the People's Republic of China, begun in December 1978. Guided by [[Deng Xiaoping]], the reforms were launched by the ruling [[Chinese Communist Party]] at its third plenary session of the 11th Central Committee on December 18, 1978, after [[Mao Zedong]]'s death in 1976. They de-collectivized agriculture, relaxed price controls, allowed foreign direct investment and created special economic zones such as [[Shenzhen]]. Private enterprises grew, while many state-owned enterprises were scaled down or privatized. China joined the [[Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation]] in 1991 and the [[World Trade Organization]] in 2001. Between 1978 and 2018 China reduced extreme poverty by 800 million. Its economy grew from $150 billion in 1978 to $18.74 trillion by 2024. Parallel political reforms of the 1980s ended with the [[1989 Tiananmen Square protests and massacre]], which halted further political liberalization.

Major branch of Protestantism, also called Calvinism, that began during the 16th-century Reformation. It emphasizes the authority of the Bible and the sovereignty of God, along with covenant theology, and uses presbyterian, congregational or some episcopal forms of church government. Articulated by [[John Calvin]], it holds to a spiritual presence of Christ in the [[Eucharist]]. The tradition began in Zürich with [[Huldrych Zwingli]] and developed especially in Switzerland, Scotland and the Netherlands. In the 17th century, followers of [[Jacobus Arminius]] were expelled from the Dutch Reformed Church over [[Predestination|predestination]] and salvation, and the resulting Canons of Dort became the basis of the so-called five points of Calvinism. Calvinism promoted hard work, trade and wealth accumulation within ethical limits, helping lay the groundwork for [[Capitalism|capitalism]] in Northern Europe and the [[United States]].

Redirection of a wave as it passes from one medium to another, caused by a change in its speed or in the medium. Refraction of [[Light|light]] is the most commonly observed type; sound and water waves also refract. The amount of bending depends on the change in wave speed and the initial direction of the wave. For light, refraction follows [[Snell's law]], which relates the sines of the angles of incidence and refraction to the [[Refractive index|refractive indices]] of the two media. Light slows in a medium such as air, glass or water, and when it enters at an angle, one side of the wavefront slows first, bending its path. Because the refractive index varies with wavelength, white light is split into colors, as in [[Prism (optics)|prisms]] and [[Rainbow|rainbows]]. The [[Human eye|human eye]] and [[Lens|lenses]] use refraction to focus light.

Problem of focusing light accurately on the retina because of the shape of the eye or cornea. The most common types are [[Myopia|near-sightedness]], far-sightedness, [[Astigmatism|astigmatism]] and presbyopia. Near-sightedness results from an eyeball that is too long, far-sightedness from one that is too short, and astigmatism from a cornea of the wrong shape. Presbyopia results from aging of the [[Lens|lens]] and affects most people over the age of 35. Diagnosis is by [[Eye examination|eye examination]], and errors are corrected with [[Glasses|eyeglasses]], contact lenses or [[Surgery|surgery]]. Eyeglasses are the easiest and safest method; contact lenses can give a wider field of vision but carry a risk of infection. An estimated 660 million people (10 per 100 people) had uncorrected refractive errors in 2013, and of these 9.5 million were blind due to the error.

Ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to its speed in a given optical medium, usually denoted n. It determines how much light bends on entering a material, as described by [[Snell's law]], and how much light is reflected at an interface. The speed and wavelength of light in a medium are reduced by the factor n, so vacuum has a refractive index of 1. Air is about 1.0003, [[Water|water]] 1.33 and [[Diamond|diamond]] 2.42. The index varies with wavelength by several percent across the visible spectrum, which causes [[Prism (optics)|dispersion]] in prisms and [[Rainbow|rainbows]]. [[Thomas Young (scientist)|Thomas Young]] probably introduced the name in 1807. Values quoted for a material must specify the wavelength used.
